questions.q: What does "onboarding" a device into Microsoft Defender for Endpoint do?
options: Registers the device with the Defender tenant so its sensor starts streaming telemetry
Installs a web server on the device
Only applies to devices running Linux, never Windows
Permanently deletes Defender Antivirus from that device
questions.explain: Before the sensor's telemetry applies to a device, that device has to be onboarded — registered with the tenant so it starts reporting.

questions.q: At real scale, how do admins typically onboard devices into Defender for Endpoint?
options: It's not possible to onboard more than one device at a time
Through Group Policy, Microsoft Intune, or Microsoft Configuration Manager, rather than one device at a time
By manually typing a registration code into every device's BIOS
Only through a phone call to Microsoft support
questions.explain: Those management tools let admins push onboarding configuration to many devices at once instead of touching each one individually.

questions.q: Which real PowerShell cmdlet reports whether Defender Antivirus real-time protection is running and signatures are current?
options: Get-ADUser
Install-WindowsFeature
Get-MpThreatDetection
Get-MpComputerStatus
questions.explain: Get-MpComputerStatus reports Defender Antivirus's current protection and signature status. Get-MpThreatDetection lists what's actually been found, a different purpose.

questions.q: Why does Defender for Endpoint correlate related alerts into a single incident?
options: Because correlation deletes the original individual alerts
Because incidents and alerts are simply two names for the exact same thing
Because a real intrusion typically produces many related alerts, often across multiple devices, and correlation gives an analyst one attack story instead of disconnected tickets
Because Microsoft limits every tenant to one alert per day
questions.explain: An attacker moving through a network triggers multiple related alerts; grouping them into one incident lets an analyst see the full attack timeline at once.

questions.q: What does automated investigation and remediation (AIR) do for a high-confidence malicious verdict?
options: It only works on devices that have never been onboarded
It emails the end user asking them to decide what to do
It always waits for a human analyst no matter how confident the verdict is
It can remediate automatically, such as quarantining a file or terminating a process, without waiting for analyst approval
questions.explain: For high-confidence malicious verdicts, AIR can act automatically. Lower-confidence verdicts get queued for analyst review instead.
